summary: Specifies how SNMP messages can be carried directly over IEEE 802 networks such as Ethernet, without IP in between. It obsoletes RFC 1089.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally the messages for managing devices ride inside internet packets. This note says they can also be put straight onto the local network wire used by Ethernet.

questions: what ethernet type does snmp use
how does snmp work without ip
subtitle: How SNMP management messages can ride straight inside Ethernet frames, with no IP underneath.

tldr.problem: Simple devices, such as the Two-Port MAC Relay being developed in IEEE 802.1, need to be managed with SNMP over a local network, but may not run a full IP stack.
tldr.mechanism: SNMP messages are serialized as in RFC 3417 and placed directly in the data portion of an IEEE 802 frame, identified by Ethernet type 33100 (hexadecimal 814C). A new transport domain, snmpIeee802Domain, names this transport.
tldr.outcome: It is an optional transport mapping that obsoletes RFC 1089 and updates RFC 3417. It only reaches devices on a single logical LAN, bridged LAN or VLAN.

today: RFC 4789 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1089 and updates RFC 3417. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4789 specifies how SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) messages can be sent directly over IEEE 802 networks. It supplements the standard SNMP transport mappings in RFC 3417 and obsoletes RFC 1089, the original SNMP over Ethernet definition.

The document also contains a small MIB module written in SMIv2. It defines no managed objects. It only defines identifiers so that other MIB modules can refer to this transport.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices on a network are checked on by a manager using a special language called SNMP. This note says that language can be spoken right on the local wire.

sections.title: Where the Mapping Applies and Its Limits
sections.content:
This is an optional transport mapping. The need was identified for managing simple devices, in applications like the Two-Port Media Access Control (MAC) Relay being developed in IEEE 802.1 as project P802.1aj.

The RFC lists inherent restrictions. Messages stay within a single logical IEEE 802 LAN, bridged LAN or VLAN. Only a single SNMP engine can be addressed on a given IEEE 802 network interface, so command generators and notification receivers, as well as command responders and notification originators, must share a single transport endpoint.
sections.plainLanguage: Notes passed this way only reach kids in the same classroom. And each desk has only one mailbox for everything coming in and going out.

sections.title: Serialization and Well-known Values
sections.content:
SNMP messages are serialized as described in Section 8 of RFC 3417. The serialized message is carried in the data portion of an IEEE LAN MAC frame.

In IEEE 802.3 frames, and other 802 frame types that can natively carry Ethernet type values, the Ethernet type 33100 (hexadecimal 814C) MUST be used as the link layer protocol identifier. In IEEE 802 LANs that use LLC to identify the protocol, such as IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs, the SNAP encapsulation method from subclause 10.5 of IEEE 802 MUST be used.

An entity using this mapping MUST be able to accept messages up to and including 484 octets. It is RECOMMENDED that implementations accept messages up to 1472 octets, and larger values are encouraged whenever possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Every package gets a special sticker, 814C, that tells the network it holds a management message. Everyone must be able to take small packages, and ideally bigger ones too.

sections.title: The IEEE 802.3 Frame Layout
sections.content:
The frame the RFC draws has four parts in order: the destination Ethernet address, the source Ethernet address, a 16-bit type field holding the value for SNMP, and then the SNMP message itself. The type field is shown in the diagram as the bits 1000000101001100, which is 814C.

No IP header or UDP header appears in this layout. The management message sits directly after the Ethernet type.
sections.plainLanguage: The frame is an envelope: who it is for, who it is from, a sticker saying what is inside, and then the message.

sections.title: The Transport Domain and Other MIB Modules
sections.content:
Several core SNMP MIB modules use TDomain/TAddress pairs to identify transport endpoints. The SNMP-TARGET-MIB uses them for notification receivers, the NOTIFICATION-LOG-MIB records the source of a notification with them, and the ENTITY-MIB uses them for the endpoint of logical entities.

The module in this RFC introduces the object identifier constant snmpIeee802Domain. It can be assigned to a TDomain object to identify an SNMP over IEEE 802 endpoint. The matching TAddress then conforms to the MacAddress textual convention, so the endpoint is simply a MAC address.
sections.plainLanguage: Other management tools keep address books. This note adds a new kind of entry whose address is a hardware address on the local network.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA made a MIB OID assignment under the snmpModules branch for the SNMP-IEEE802-TM-MIB module. IANA also assigned an OID value below snmpDomains for the transport domain, which first required setting up a registry for OIDs under snmpDomains (prefix 1.3.6.1.6.1).

The new domain, snmpIeee802Domain, took value 6, after five existing entries for UDP, CLNS, CONS, DDP and IPX. New assignments require a specification, as per RFC 2434.
sections.plainLanguage: A librarian keeps a numbered list of transports. This one was added as number six.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module defines no management objects, only an OBJECT-IDENTIFIER, so the RFC says it has no impact on the security of the Internet. Meaningful security considerations can only be written in the MIB modules that define management objects.

SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c messages are not considered secure. Implementors are advised to consider SNMPv3 messages, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 3414) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 3415). It is the customer's or user's responsibility to configure the SNMP entity so that only principals with legitimate rights can GET or SET the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The old versions of SNMP are like talking out loud in a crowd. The newer version adds secret codes and a list of who may do what.
